title: The Survey Course: from Kiryat Ata to a Brief History of Humankind
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Kiryat Ata, and a Map of Europe on the Floor

stops.name: Kiryat Ata, the youngest of three
stops.date_confidence: attested; birth date and town confirmed by Hebrew Wikipedia and by the English Wikipedia article on Kiryat Ata, which lists him among the town's notable natives. Some secondary sources say 'Haifa' as regional shorthand. Coordinates are the town centre, not a street address. The grandparents' origins are family history relayed by Hebrew Wikipedia, not archival records; the precise 1 December 1921 birth date for the grandmother comes from a family tribute post and is not independently verified.
stops.campa: In Kiryat Ata, an industrial town in the hills behind Haifa, a third child is born into a secular Jewish family with two daughters already. The father is an engineer at Rafael, the state weapons developer, and the surname is an adopted Hebrew one: he was born Blajberg, which Hebrew sources render Bleiberg. The mother's parents come from further off, a grandmother born in Halberstadt in 1921 to a Polish Jewish family, a grandfather from Czernowitz who served in the British Army as a Jewish Palestinian. The town will later list the boy among its notable natives, under author and historian.
suggested_refs: Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, the state armaments developer that employed Shlomo Harari

stops.name: Haifa, Leo Baeck and the two buses
stops.date_confidence: the school is attested in both the English and Hebrew Wikipedia articles; the age of about eight, the two bus journeys each way, and the floor map of Europe come from Ian Parker's 2020 New Yorker profile as relayed by the working dossier, which could not be refetched this session because newyorker.com blocked the request. The month and day are placeholders. Coordinates are a general Haifa placement, not a verified street address for the school.
stops.campa: From about the age of eight he is enrolled in the programme for gifted children at the Leo Baeck Education Center in Haifa. That means two bus journeys each way from Kiryat Ata, every school day, at both ends of the lessons. He reads early and out of order, and what he is raised beside is a canon of texts rather than of images. At home a room's floor is given over to a large map of Europe, and he fights historical campaigns across it, moving armies through terrain he has never stood on. The buses run between an industrial town and a school in Haifa. The rest of the continent is on the floor.
suggested_refs: The Leo Baeck Education Center, Haifa, and its programme for gifted children
sources: Ian Parker, 'Yuval Noah Harari's History of Everyone, Ever', The New Yorker, 10 February 2020, via the working dossier

stops.name: Kiryat Ata, the Intifada at eleven
stops.date_confidence: the December 1987 outbreak of the First Intifada is general historical record. Harari's own description of his adolescent politics as right-wing and nationalist is carried from the New Yorker profile via the dossier and could not be verified directly, the article being paywalled and unfetchable this session. The academic reserve track is stated in the geography material; no enlistment document was located.
stops.campa: The First Intifada breaks out in December, and he is eleven. He will describe the politics of his adolescence afterward as right-wing and nationalist, the ordinary settings of an Israeli boy in the years when the occupied territories turn from an administrative arrangement into a running war. His military obligation is later deferred into the academic reserve track, which sends him to a lecture hall instead of a unit; he will spend fifteen years on soldiers' memoirs without ever acquiring one of his own. When his politics changed, and what changed them, nothing in the reachable record says.
suggested_refs: The atuda academic reserve track of the Israel Defense Forces
sources: Ian Parker, The New Yorker, 10 February 2020, via the working dossier

stops.name: Mount Scopus, matriculation at seventeen
stops.date_confidence: the 1993-1998 Hebrew University degree is attested by Hebrew Wikipedia and the university's own history department page; the month is a placeholder for the Israeli academic year. The coordinate is the canonical Mount Scopus pin inherited byte-identical from the Einstein journey. Wikipedia's own figure for the Mount Scopus campus is 31.7944 by 35.2389, and the Buber journey carries the same pin with a corrected campus position of 31.7936 by 35.2447; the divergence is recorded rather than resolved.
stops.campa: He enters the Hebrew University of Jerusalem at about seventeen, in the reserve track that defers conscription for a degree, and reads history with international relations. Five years on Mount Scopus, a hill that stood cut off from Jewish Jerusalem for nineteen years before it was recovered. He chooses medieval and Renaissance Europe: crusader cavalry, siege parties, the men who wrote down what they saw. Not the twentieth century, and not this country, and not any period in which a living person could contradict a witness. He is seventeen when he starts, and the degree runs to 1998.
suggested_refs: The Hebrew University's Mount Scopus campus and its department of history

stops.name: Mount Scopus, the Frankish turcopoles
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to detail. The article 'The Military Role of the Frankish Turcopoles: A Reassessment' in Mediterranean Historical Review 12(1), 75-116, 1997, is carried from the dossier's journal citation; the journal record could not be fetched this session to confirm the pagination or the month. That it grew out of undergraduate work is the dossier's account.
stops.campa: An undergraduate paper becomes his first real article: The Military Role of the Frankish Turcopoles: A Reassessment, on the light cavalry the crusader states raised from local converts and hired horsemen. The turcopoles are the unclassifiable soldiers of those kingdoms, neither Frankish nor Muslim, and the historiography had largely filed them away without opening the file. He takes a category everybody uses and asks what is inside it, the move he will still be making thirty years later on much larger material. He is twenty-one. Mediterranean Historical Review, volume twelve, number one, pages seventy-five to one hundred and sixteen.
suggested_refs: Mediterranean Historical Review 12(1), 1997, 'The Military Role of the Frankish Turcopoles: A Reassessment'
sources: Working dossier, citing Mediterranean Historical Review 12(1), 75-116

stops.name: Jesus College, Oxford, the doctoral years
stops.date_confidence: attested: Hebrew Wikipedia and the Hebrew University history department page both give Jesus College, Oxford, 1998-2002, under Steven Gunn. The month is the Michaelmas placeholder. Coordinates from Wikipedia, 'Jesus College, Oxford'.
stops.campa: He goes to Jesus College for the doctorate, supervised by Steven Gunn, and spends four years inside Renaissance military memoirs written between about 1450 and 1600. What happened in the battles is not the question. What the men who fought them believed the fighting had taught them is, and why they held that having been present conferred an authority no reader could challenge. The claim he is tracking is the one his subjects make in their own defence: that a man who was not there has nothing to say about it. He is reading them at a desk in an English library, five hundred years late.
suggested_refs: Steven J. Gunn's Tudor military and political history, the supervisory context of the thesis

stops.name: Soho, London, the false liberation
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction throughout. The clubs, the MDMA on several occasions, the dating of men and the coming out during the Oxford years come from Harari's own interviews as relayed by the dossier via the New Yorker profile, unfetchable this session. No source names a district, a venue or a year; Soho stands as the generic centre of London gay nightlife in this period, and the date is an ordering device only.
stops.campa: Weekends carry him from Oxford down to London, to the clubs, to Ecstasy taken on a handful of occasions, to men. He comes out as gay in these years, at a distance from Kiryat Ata and from everyone who knew him there. False liberation is his own phrase for it afterward: the constraint lifted, and the unhappiness stayed exactly where it had been sitting. No source names a street, a venue or a year. Soho is standing in for a district here, not marking a place he is known to have been.
suggested_refs: Harari's own published accounts of coming out during his Oxford years
sources: Working dossier, drawing on Ian Parker, The New Yorker, 10 February 2020, and Harari interviews

stops.name: Herefordshire, ten days of silence
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The dossier places a first ten-day Vipassana retreat in the S. N. Goenka tradition in western England in 2000, introduced by his friend Ron Merom, and attributes it to the New Yorker profile and Harari's interviews; neither could be fetched directly this session. The dossier does not name a centre. Dhamma Dipa in Herefordshire is offered as the best-known Goenka-tradition site in western England, a plausible identification only, and the coordinates are approximate.
stops.campa: A friend, Ron Merom, a software engineer, tells him to try a ten-day Vipassana course in the S. N. Goenka tradition. He goes, somewhere in western England, and for ten days does nothing but watch the breath enter and leave the nostrils and observe sensation cross the body without reacting to any of it. He is a doctoral student writing about men who insist that experience cannot be transmitted in words. The retreat proposes that experience can be observed directly, by anyone, using no words at all. He will go back every year for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The S. N. Goenka Vipassana tradition and its ten-day course structure
sources: Working dossier, citing Ian Parker, The New Yorker, and Harari interviews

stops.name: Toronto, the civil ceremony
stops.date_confidence: the Toronto civil marriage is attested by English Wikipedia, which also states the reason plainly: Israel recognises civil marriages, same sex or opposite sex, only when conducted abroad. Some profiles give 2001 and some 2002; Wikipedia dates the marriage to 2002 and that is used here rather than the dossier's open range. The City Hall venue is an unsourced inference and the coordinate is Toronto City Hall as a civic placeholder; no source names the building. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: He and Itzik Yahav marry in a civil ceremony in Toronto. Israel has no civil marriage at all, for anybody, and recognises only marriages conducted abroad, so an Israeli couple of the same sex who want a legal marriage buy two plane tickets. They come home married under a law they had to leave the country to reach. Yahav will become his manager, his business partner and the co-founder of the company they run together, and the dedication of 21 Lessons for the 21st Century is to him.
suggested_refs: Israeli law on marriages conducted abroad and their domestic registration

stops.name: Sheldonian Theatre, Oxford, the doctorate conferred
stops.date_confidence: the DPhil in 2002 and the thesis title are attested by the Hebrew University history department page and Hebrew Wikipedia. The venue is a reconstruction from standard Oxford practice: no source consulted names the ceremony location, the date, or whether he attended in person. Coordinates corrected to Wikipedia's figure for the Sheldonian, 51.7543 by 1.2550 west. Month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Oxford confers the doctorate in history for a thesis titled History and I: War and the Relations Between History and Personal Identity in Renaissance Military Memoirs, c. 1450-1600. He is twenty-six. Under the painted ceiling of Wren's theatre, where the university has capped its doctors since the seventeenth century, authority is conferred by procedure and costume rather than by having been present, which is the whole subject of the thesis being capped. No source records which day, or whether he was in the room.
suggested_refs: The Sheldonian Theatre, customary site of Oxford degree conferrals

stops.name: Mount Scopus, the post in the history department
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia for the 2003 return and the Yad Hanadiv postdoctoral fellowship of 2003-2005. That the survey course dates from 2003 comes from ynharari.com. Month and day unknown. The coordinate is the canonical Mount Scopus pin inherited from the Einstein journey; see the divergence noted at the 1993 stop.
stops.campa: He comes back to Jerusalem and to the department he graduated from, on a Yad Hanadiv postdoctoral fellowship running to 2005, and then he stays. The teaching includes a broad survey of world history from 2003 onward, the sort of course a department hands to whoever will take it: the whole species, from the first stone tools to the present, in one academic year. It is not a prestigious assignment and nobody else wants it. He takes it, and goes on teaching it for seven years to undergraduates on Mount Scopus, unnoticed by anybody outside the building.
suggested_refs: The Yad Hanadiv postdoctoral fellowship scheme

stops.name: Jerusalem, the three books on war
stops.date_confidence: publication years from English Wikipedia: Renaissance Military Memoirs 2004, Special Operations in the Age of Chivalry 2007, The Ultimate Experience 2008. Wikipedia carries the 2007 title as attested and the 2004 and 2008 titles with less corroboration; all three are here on Wikipedia's authority alone, no publisher record having been fetched. The stop is dated to the first of the three and covers all three; months unknown.
stops.campa: Renaissance Military Memoirs appears in 2004, out of the thesis. Special Operations in the Age of Chivalry follows in 2007, on medieval raids and assassinations carried out by very small numbers of men. The Ultimate Experience comes in 2008 and is the largest of them, subtitled Battlefield Revelations and the Making of Modern War Culture: five and a half centuries of soldiers claiming that battle revealed to them something no other route could teach. These are specialist books with specialist print runs, reviewed by other specialists.
suggested_refs: The Ultimate Experience: Battlefield Revelations and the Making of Modern War Culture, 1450-2000 (2008)

stops.name: Igatpuri, thirty days and sixty days
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The annual long retreats of thirty to sixty days, the assistant-teacher role and the dedication of Homo Deus to S. N. Goenka come from the dossier, which places the retreats 'often in India'. No source consulted names Dhamma Giri at Igatpuri in connection with Harari; the town is confirmed by Wikipedia as the seat of the Goenka movement and is used as the most likely single site. The date is an ordering device for a recurring practice, not a specific retreat.
stops.campa: Once a year the academic disappears. Thirty days, sometimes sixty, of Vipassana, often in India, in the country that grew up around S. N. Goenka in the hills at Igatpuri: no reading, no writing, no telephone, no speech. He will eventually qualify as an assistant teacher in the tradition, and will dedicate Homo Deus to Goenka for teaching him to observe things as they are. The books get written in the eleven months left over. He has said that without the practice he could not have written them at all.
suggested_refs: Dhamma Giri, the Vipassana International Academy at Igatpuri, Maharashtra

stops.name: Jerusalem, the prizes of a mid-career academic
stops.date_confidence: the Polonsky Prizes of 2009 and 2012 and the Young Israeli Academy of Sciences election of 2012 are attested by English Wikipedia. The 2011 Society for Military History award is confirmed by English Wikipedia as the Moncado Award, not the 'Moncado Prize' the dossier called it. The stop is dated to the first award and covers the run; months unknown.
stops.campa: The Hebrew University gives him its Polonsky Prize for Creativity and Originality in 2009, and again in 2012. The Society for Military History gives him a Moncado Award in 2011. The Young Israeli Academy of Sciences elects him in 2012. These are the honours of a successful mid-career academic in a small and technical field, given by the people who read technical work, and none of them is reported outside the university. The survey course keeps running through all of it.
suggested_refs: The Polonsky Prize for Creativity and Originality, Hebrew University of Jerusalem

stops.name: Mount Scopus, the notes become a book
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the father's death, which the dossier dates to 2010 during the composition of Sapiens; no death record was located and the date could not be independently confirmed, though it is consistent with the timeline. That the book grew from the survey course is attested by ynharari.com. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: He begins turning the world-history survey into a book, written in Hebrew, for Israeli readers, with no expectation of a foreign edition. His father dies while he is writing it. Shlomo Harari, the engineer at Rafael, does not live to see what the lecture notes become. The argument taking shape is that the things holding large numbers of strangers together, money and nations and corporations and gods, are none of them found in nature, and are none of them simply lies either. They are real in the only way that counts, because enough people act as though they were.
suggested_refs: The Hebrew University world-history survey course, taught from 2003

stops.name: Israel, Dvir prints Qitsur Toldot ha-Enoshut
stops.date_confidence: the 2011 Hebrew edition from Dvir Publishing House is attested by English Wikipedia's article on Sapiens. The dossier's 'June 2011' is unsourced and is dropped; the month here is a placeholder. The coordinate is a Tel Aviv metropolitan placeholder and is a poor proxy: Dvir trades within Kinneret Zmora-Dvir, whose offices are in Or Yehuda, not central Tel Aviv, and no verified street address was obtained.
stops.campa: Dvir publishes Qitsur Toldot ha-Enoshut, A Brief History of Humankind, in Hebrew, and it becomes an Israeli bestseller. The book is written for a few million readers in a language almost none of its eventual audience can read. Its central claim is about the machinery of belief: that Homo sapiens took the planet not through strength or intelligence but through the capacity to coordinate in very large numbers around stories with no referent outside the telling. It sells, in Hebrew, in Israel, in the year it appears. Why that argument found its first mass readership in that country is not a question anybody seems to have put to him.
stops.quote: How do you cause people to believe in an imagined order such as Christianity, democracy or capitalism? First, you never admit that the order is imagined.
stops.quote_source: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind (Harper, English edition 2014). The imagined-order argument belongs to the chapter 'Building Pyramids'; the Wikiquote compilation's chapter attribution for this line is unreliable and no chapter is asserted here.
suggested_refs: Dvir Publishing House and the Kinneret Zmora-Dvir group, Or Yehuda
sources: Wikipedia, 'Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind'

stops.name: Tel Aviv, From Animals Into Gods
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia's Sapiens article, which names the 2012 self-published print-on-demand English translation From Animals Into Gods and its sale of fewer than two thousand copies. The title is information the working dossier lacked. Month unknown; the coordinate is a generic Tel Aviv placement, no publishing address being involved in a print-on-demand issue.
stops.campa: Before any agent takes him on, he and Yahav translate the book into English themselves and put it out print-on-demand under a different title, From Animals Into Gods. It sells fewer than two thousand copies. Two years later the same argument, professionally edited and auctioned in London, will sell in the millions. Nothing inside the text changes in between. What changes is the apparatus around it, which happens to be the subject of the text. The self-published edition is still findable secondhand.
stops.quote: Money is the most universal and most efficient system of mutual trust ever devised.
stops.quote_source: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind, chapter 10, 'The Scent of Money' (Harper, English edition 2014; Hebrew original 2011)
suggested_refs: From Animals Into Gods (self-published, 2012), the print-on-demand English text
sources: Wikipedia, 'Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind'

stops.name: London, the auction and the English Sapiens
stops.date_confidence: the 2014 English edition is attested by English Wikipedia, which credits Random House and Harper. The agent Deborah Harris, the 2013 London auction and the Harvill Secker imprint are dossier-only: Wikipedia's Sapiens article contains no mention of Harris, of an auction or of 2013, and attributing that chain to Wikipedia would be a citation error. The endorsers named on Wikipedia are Bill Gates and Mark Zuckerberg; Barack Obama's praise is real but separate, dating to 2016, and is not in the cited source. The coordinate is central London, no verified publisher address having been obtained. Month unknown.
stops.campa: The literary agent Deborah Harris takes on international rights and the book goes to auction in London in 2013. Random House and Harper acquire it, and Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind appears in English in 2014 under the Harvill Secker imprint. Bill Gates and Mark Zuckerberg recommend it in public. A book arguing that information networks run on shared fiction is carried outward by two men who own information networks, and the argument travels on exactly the machinery it describes. Editions follow in one language after another.
stops.quote: Money is more open-minded than language, state laws, cultural codes, religious beliefs and social habits. Money is the only trust system created by humans that can bridge almost any cultural gap, and that does not discriminate on the basis of religion, gender, race, age or sexual orientation.
stops.quote_source: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind, chapter 10, 'The Scent of Money' (Harper, English edition 2014)
suggested_refs: The Deborah Harris Agency, Jerusalem, and the 2013 international rights auction
sources: Wikipedia, 'Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind'
Working dossier for the agent and auction

stops.name: New York, the American reception and the reviewers
stops.date_confidence: the slower initial American sales are the dossier's account and were not independently verified. The Hallpike and Narayanan criticisms are attested by English Wikipedia's Sapiens article, which quotes both; Narayanan is identified there as a neuroscientist, correcting the dossier's 'cognitive scientist'. Hallpike's sentence is quoted here as Wikipedia renders it, without the dossier's trailing clause 'sometimes seriously', which does not appear there. Coordinates are HarperCollins's publicly known Lower Manhattan address, not re-verified. Month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: The American edition moves slowly at first, more slowly than in Britain and across Europe, until the endorsements catch up with it. The academic response is harder than the popular one. The anthropologist Christopher Hallpike reviews it and finds a book whose correct facts are not new and whose new claims are not correct. The neuroscientist Darshana Narayanan returns to it in 2022 and writes that the errors are numerous and substantial and cannot be dismissed as nit-picking. The sales figures do not register either of them.
stops.quote: whenever his facts are broadly correct they are not new, and whenever he tries to strike out on his own he often gets things wrong.
stops.quote_source: C. R. Hallpike, review of Sapiens, as quoted in Wikipedia, 'Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind'
suggested_refs: C. R. Hallpike's published review of Sapiens; Darshana Narayanan's 2022 critique
sources: Wikipedia, 'Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind'

stops.name: Beijing, the Wenjin Book Award
stops.date_confidence: attested: ynharari.com/about lists '2015: China's Wenjin Book Award (Sapiens)', which upgrades the dossier's tentative account. The National Library of China awards the Wenjin Prize and is the correct venue; its coordinates are corrected here to Wikipedia's figure of 39.9459 by 116.3224, the dossier's 39.9346 by 116.3372 being about 1.9 km off. The CITIC author of the year designation is dated 2020 by ynharari.com. Month unknown.
stops.campa: The National Library of China gives Sapiens its Wenjin Book Award, and the publisher CITIC will later name him its author of the year in China. A book whose thesis is that empires and money and religions all run on collective belief is honoured by the national library of a state that treats the management of collective belief as a first-order administrative function. Chinese sales run into the millions. He has never publicly explained how he squares that reception with the rest of what he argues.
stops.quote: religion has been the third great unifier of humankind, alongside money and empires.
stops.quote_source: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind, chapter 12, 'The Law of Religion' (Harper, English edition 2014)
suggested_refs: The Wenjin Book Award of the National Library of China

stops.name: Tel Aviv, Homo Deus
stops.date_confidence: attested: Hebrew edition from Dvir in 2015, English from Harvill Secker in September 2016 and in the United States in February 2017, per English Wikipedia. The dossier's claim that the book introduced the term 'Dataism' is dropped: the term was coined by David Brooks in a 2013 New York Times column and Wikipedia does not credit Harari with it. Coordinates are a generic Tel Aviv placement.
stops.campa: Homo Deus: A Brief History of Tomorrow comes out in Hebrew from Dvir in 2015 and in English the following September. The premise is that famine, plague and war have been demoted from acts of God to manageable problems, and that a species which has solved those turns next to immortality, engineered happiness and divinity. It also carries a warning about Dataism, the belief that the universe is a flow of data and that a thing's worth is its contribution to processing. The word is not his. David Brooks coined it in a newspaper column in 2013, and Harari borrows it in order to argue against it.
stops.quote: Capitalism did not defeat communism because capitalism was more ethical, because individual liberties are sacred or because God was angry with the heathen communists. Rather, capitalism won the Cold War because distributed data processing works better than centralised data processing, at least in periods of accelerating technological change.
stops.quote_source: Homo Deus: A Brief History of Tomorrow (Random House, 2016)
suggested_refs: David Brooks, 'The Philosophy of Data', The New York Times, 2013, where the term Dataism is coined

stops.name: Dusseldorf, the German Economic Book Award
stops.date_confidence: attested: ynharari.com/about confirms '2017: Handelsblatt's German Economic Book Award (Homo Deus)', which upgrades the dossier's tentative tagging. No source identifies the ceremony venue or date; the coordinate is a generic Dusseldorf city-centre placement at the newspaper's home city, and the month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Handelsblatt gives Homo Deus its German Economic Book Award. The prize is for economics writing and the book is not an economics book; what it brings to the category is an account of money as a technology of belief rather than a medium of exchange, and German business readers give it a prize for saying so. No source names the hall, the date or anyone who was in the room. Dusseldorf is where the newspaper is, and that is as close as the record comes.
stops.quote: In modern society, currency notes usually display religious images, revered ancestors and corporate totems.
stops.quote_source: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind, chapter 2, 'The Tree of Knowledge' (Harper, English edition 2014)
suggested_refs: The Handelsblatt Deutscher Wirtschaftsbuchpreis

stops.name: Cambridge, the fellowship in existential risk
stops.date_confidence: the Distinguished Research Fellowship at the Centre for the Study of Existential Risk is carried from the dossier; no CSER page was fetched this session to confirm the title or its start date. The date here is an ordering device only, the appointment being described in the material as ongoing rather than dated. Coordinates are the dossier's CSER placement in Cambridge.
stops.campa: He is made a Distinguished Research Fellow at the Centre for the Study of Existential Risk, an institute founded to think in an organised way about how the species might end. The man appointed to it wrote his doctorate on medieval raiding parties. Public profiles regularly compress the post into a professorship at Jerusalem and Cambridge; it is a fellowship, it carries no chair and no teaching, and the compression flatters it. The centre's own page was not reachable, and when the appointment began is not established anywhere the record can be checked.
suggested_refs: The Centre for the Study of Existential Risk, University of Cambridge

stops.name: Davos, the address on nationalism and data
stops.date_confidence: the 2018 World Economic Forum address is carried from the dossier; no transcript was fetched this session. Coordinates corrected to Wikipedia's figure for the Davos Congress Centre, 46.8007 by 9.8314, the dossier's 46.8021 by 9.8368 being about 430 m off; the same correction applies to every Davos stop in this file. Month is the customary January meeting, day unknown.
stops.campa: At the Congress Centre in Davos he tells the World Economic Forum that the danger ahead is not the old totalitarianism but a new efficiency: gather enough biometric and behavioural data, process it well enough, and a regime can know a citizen better than that citizen knows himself. The old dictatorships had to guess at what people wanted, and could be wrong for decades at a time; this one would not have to guess. In the room are the assembled owners of exactly that data. He will be back in this hall in 2026 with a harder version of the same warning.
stops.quote: In the twenty-first century we will create more powerful fictions and more totalitarian religions than in any previous era. With the help of biotechnology and computer algorithms these religions will not only control our minute-by-minute existence, but will be able to shape our bodies, brains and minds, and to create entire virtual worlds complete with hells and heavens.
stops.quote_source: Homo Deus: A Brief History of Tomorrow (Random House, 2016)
suggested_refs: The Davos Congress Centre, host of the World Economic Forum's annual meetings since 1971

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the body that stays behind
stops.date_confidence: attested that he appeared at TED2018 live from Tel Aviv as a digital projection, per English Wikipedia and the TED talk page. The specific studio is not identified in any source consulted and the coordinate is generic Tel Aviv centre. Day unknown.
stops.campa: For TED2018 he does not fly. He stands in a studio in Tel Aviv and lets his image be thrown live onto a stage in Canada, in what is described as the first TED talk delivered by an avatar. His actual body spends the talk some nine thousand kilometres from the audience applauding it. The subject of the talk is what happens when the data about a person becomes more usable than the person. The arrangement is reported everywhere as a first, and the studio is named nowhere reachable.
suggested_refs: The TED2018 telepresence staging, described as the conference's first avatar talk
sources: ted.com talk page for 'Why Fascism Is So Tempting, and How Your Data Could Power It'

stops.name: Vancouver Convention Centre, the figure on the stage
stops.date_confidence: the talk and its title are attested by the TED talk page; the Vancouver venue for TED2018 is well documented. Coordinates corrected to Wikipedia's figure for the Vancouver Convention Centre at 1055 Canada Place, 49.2892 by -123.1139, the dossier's 49.287 by -123.117 drifting about 250 m. The exact day of the talk within the April conference week is not confirmed.
stops.campa: In the hall on Canada Place the talk is titled Why Fascism Is So Tempting, and How Your Data Could Power It. He separates nationalism, which he defends as the human capacity to care about millions of strangers, from fascism, which he describes as the belief that one's own nation is the only thing that matters. Then he moves to the practical question: what a state can do once it holds enough biometric data on enough people. The figure standing on the stage is made of light.
stops.quote: Democracy in its present form cannot survive the merger of biotech and infotech. Either democracy will successfully reinvent itself in a radically new form, or humans will come to live in 'digital dictatorships'.
stops.quote_source: 21 Lessons for the 21st Century (Spiegel & Grau / Jonathan Cape, 2018)
suggested_refs: TED2018, 'Why Fascism Is So Tempting, and How Your Data Could Power It'

stops.name: Tel Aviv, 21 Lessons and the dedication
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia for the 2018 publication, the subject matter and the dedication to his husband. Month is the publication month reported for the English edition and is not independently confirmed here; day unknown. Coordinates are a generic Tel Aviv placement, the publishers being in London and New York.
stops.campa: 21 Lessons for the 21st Century is the third book and the least historical of them: work, liberty, nationalism, religion, immigration, terrorism, meaning, meditation, addressed to a reader alive right now rather than to a period. The dedication is to Itzik Yahav, married in Toronto sixteen years earlier.
